flashcards.q: Is TypeScript's type system structural or nominal? What does that mean?
flashcards.a: Structural -- two types are compatible if their shapes match, regardless of declared name or inheritance. An object literal can satisfy an interface it never declared implementing.

flashcards.q: When does the excess property check fire, and when doesn't it?
flashcards.a: Fires on object literals passed directly to a typed parameter (catches likely typos). Does NOT fire on variables holding an object with genuinely extra properties.

flashcards.q: What does 'types are erased' mean and what's the practical consequence?
flashcards.a: Every type annotation/interface/generic is deleted at compile time -- zero runtime trace. TypeScript can never enforce anything at runtime; values crossing unchecked boundaries (as assertions, untyped imports, stale .d.ts files) can be structurally wrong while the checker reports everything fine.

Both accept any assigned value. any disables type checking entirely for anything it touches (propagates silently). unknown requires explicit narrowing (typeof/instanceof/guard) before any operation is permitted.

flashcards.q: Why is a discriminated union better than one flat interface with optional fields for state?
flashcards.a: A flat interface allows illegal combinations to compile (e.g. loading:true with stale data present). A discriminated union with a literal tag field makes such combinations structurally impossible -- fields only exist in the branch's type where they're valid.

flashcards.q: How do you force the compiler to catch an unhandled discriminated union variant?
flashcards.a: const _exhaustive: never = value in the default/fallback branch of a switch -- if a new variant is unhandled, value isn't assignable to never, producing a compile error.

flashcards.q: Why is an `as` type assertion dangerous?
flashcards.a: It performs zero runtime verification -- if the value isn't actually shaped as claimed, the assertion compiles fine and the mismatch surfaces later, often far downstream from the actual bad assumption.

flashcards.q: What is function parameter bivariance and what flag addresses it?
flashcards.a: Without strictFunctionTypes, a function type (x:Dog)=>void is assignable to (x:Animal)=>void and vice versa, even though only contravariance is actually safe. strictFunctionTypes fixes this for standalone function types, but method syntax remains bivariant even under strict mode.

flashcards.q: What is declaration merging, a legitimate use, and its risk?
flashcards.a: Multiple interface declarations with the same name across files auto-merge into one. Legitimate use: augmenting global/third-party types (e.g. adding a property to Window). Risk: it declares a runtime shape exists with zero verification anything actually sets it.

flashcards.q: Implement Pick<T,K> and Partial<T> as mapped types from first principles.
flashcards.a: Pick<T,K> = { [P in K]: T[P] } (with K extends keyof T). Partial<T> = { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] }.

flashcards.q: As of TypeScript 4.4+, what type do caught errors in a catch clause default to, and why?
flashcards.a: unknown, under useUnknownInCatchVariables (on by default in strict mode) -- because a thrown value's actual type is never knowable ahead of time; any was the historically incorrect default.

flashcards.q: What changed in TypeScript 6.0 (March 2026) and what is TypeScript 7.0?
flashcards.a: 6.0 was the last release on the original JS-based compiler, flipping defaults toward stricter mode, ESM default module, es2025 target. 7.0 is a from-scratch Go rewrite of the compiler, reported ~10x faster, reaching RC June 18 2026 -- same language semantics, faster tooling.
